subjects.displayTitle: Divine grace, bounty, confirmations and spiritual capacity
subjects.introduction: How can grace be a free gift and still depend on capacity and effort? These 300 chosen quotations include every verified authorized selection in the compilation. They open with the ceaseless outpouring of divine bounty and its seeming delays, then present grace as given beyond merit, with faith, guidance and recognition singled out as pure bestowal. Passages on capacity and receptivity explain why the same rain makes one ground a garden and leaves another barren. The readings then show how fully human effort depends on confirmation, and name what attracts it, such as teaching, pure intention, love, unity, steadfastness and thankfulness, as well as what cuts it off. A long sequence presents the transformation of the weak, the drop into an ocean and the ant into a Solomon, and finds confirmation increased by trial. Promises of the hosts on high and accounts of assistance follow, and prayers close the linked readings. An authorized prayer asks God not to leave His servants to themselves [1], and an authorized extract hopes for success by the grace and favour of God [2]. Many quotations are reported talks and keep that status. The actual neighboring subjects connect this study with angels, the Concourse on high, confirmation and enkindlement in teaching, the development and differences of capacity, and the forgiveness and mercy of God.

Here grace is presented as a gift that no one earns. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes that the blessings of the Abhá Kingdom do not depend on capacity or worthiness, for the blessings themselves become the worthiness, and that this is the Day of Grace rather than the Day of Justice. Faith, guidance and recognition are singled out as pure bestowal: one soul finds the path by the flame of a lamp while another misses it in sunlight, and souls who spent years in worship and learning remained deprived. Other passages qualify the claim. One distinguishes gifts gained through effort and capability from those that are pure bounty; another says that every bounty follows capacity except faith and certitude. Bahá’u’lláh adds that good deeds without divine acceptance are sheer nothingness. How can grace be universal and also specific? What follows from having received freely?

The rain of grace takes on the limits of the ground where it falls, yields nothing on brackish soil and turns pure soil into a garden; the rays of the sun appear only in a polished mirror. Iron is drawn from afar while earth remains unmoved close by. Several passages treat capacity as something to be developed: by plowing the soil, by thirst, by detachment, love and unity, and by prayer for receptiveness. Others speak of capacity that differs by nature, and of the second birth as the capacity to receive the bestowals of God. A recipient who is unaware of a gift, like a child with a gem, gains little from it. Many items here are reported talks. How do these passages fit with the claim that grace does not depend on capacity? What would developing capacity involve?

These readings insist that human effort, however necessary, cannot succeed alone. Without confirmation every water becomes fire, learning in every science accomplishes little, education does not succeed, and no soul can draw a breath or take a step; were God’s glance withdrawn, all would return to nothingness. Healing and commerce are each given a material and a spiritual cause. Two passages see confirmation at work in history: martyrs moved by a breeze that onlookers mistook for their own power, and the sun as a single sign that conquers the world. How can a person rely wholly on confirmation and still act responsibly? What is left to the rudder?

Many passages name what draws confirmation, often through the image of a magnet. Teaching the Cause is called the magnet of confirmation, and one reported talk says that confirmations cease when teaching is suspended. Pure intention, real love, benevolent intentions, unity and agreement, firmness, detachment, humility, patience, dignity and thankfulness are also named, together with service in schools, Assemblies, gatherings and the building of a House of Worship. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that one step taken in the path of truth brings confirmations in succession, while a foreordained bestowal still needs effort to become real. Other passages name what shuts confirmation off: discord, weariness and the search for rest, a depressed mind, pride, and conduct that blocks the outpourings for others. Any deficiency, one Tablet says, arises from our own shortcoming. Do these conditions compete with the gift of grace, or prepare for it? Which is most within reach today?

Pure intention, real love, benevolent intentions, unity and agreement, firmness, detachment, humility, patience, dignity and thankfulness are also named, together with service in schools, Assemblies, gatherings and the building of a House of Worship. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá adds that one step taken in the path of truth brings confirmations in succession, while a foreordained bestowal still needs effort to become real. Other passages name what shuts confirmation off: discord, weariness and the search for rest, a depressed mind, pride, and conduct that blocks the outpourings for others. Any deficiency, one Tablet says, arises from our own shortcoming. Do these conditions compete with the gift of grace, or prepare for it? Which is most within reach today?

The most frequent image in the compilation is transformation: a drop becomes an ocean, an atom a sun, a seed a tree, an ant a Solomon and a gnat an eagle. These passages answer a reader’s sense of weakness. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá counsels looking not at one’s own capacity but at the favors of Bahá’u’lláh, and reported talks recall how Mary, through her love of Christ, was given every capacity, and how a soul unable to teach became eloquent when sent forth. Bahá’u’lláh bids the weak, the sick and the weary seek wealth, healing and utterance through His Names. A connected group turns to trial: confirmations increase with opposition, the fiercer the troubles the more intense the succor, and poverty, loss and abasement in the path of God become wealth, profit and glory. If comfort were available, one passage asks, where would distinction in striving appear? How does looking away from one’s weakness differ from denying it?

These readings record promises of assistance and accounts of it. Bahá’u’lláh writes that whoever arises to serve Him, He will arise to assist, and that God has prescribed for Himself the assistance of those who convey His Cause; the Báb gives a promise of assistance binding upon God. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes the hosts of the Concourse on high arrayed and waiting for a soul to step into the arena of service, and explains elsewhere that angels signify the power of the confirmations of God. Bahá’u’lláh recalls words heard in a dream: We shall render Thee victorious by Thyself and by Thy Pen. Reported talks recount ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s journeys, where He attributes every opened door to confirmation, and a Tablet describes confirmations vouchsafed day after day to friends who raised a House of Worship in fellowship. Read promise and testimony together. What does a promise of hosts ask of the one who receives it? How might a person recognize confirmation in their own service?

The linked readings close with prayers. Several turn the teaching on capacity into petition: Do not look upon our capabilities, but deal with us according to Thy infinite Mercy; Cast me not out of the presence of Thy grace. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá prays as one who is poor, ignorant and dead, asking for wealth, knowledge and the breath of life. Others ask for confirmation in service, for strength in obedience, and that fire and sorrow be turned into light and joy. Two prayers of Bahá’u’lláh begin Aware as I am, O my God, acknowledging what God has already ordained for His servants, and still ask. The Báb gives thanks that neither trials nor His own shortcomings kept Him from praising God. What changes when a teaching becomes a prayer? Which petition speaks most directly to your own need?

This authorized prayer of Bahá’u’lláh is supplied without Thy before knowledge; the omission remains as given, and the approximate status is preserved. The complete prayer begins O my God! O my God! Unite the hearts of Thy servants and asks that they follow His commandments and be helped in their endeavor. Read the whole prayer at the linked source. How does the plea that God not leave His servants to themselves gather the readings on grace and dependence?

Only the words after the ellipsis are authorized. The salutation O seeker after confirmation comes from a paragraph outside the authorized range and remains as supplied. In the authorized extract ‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes that a child taking examinations may succeed by the grace and favour of God and go on to study agriculture. Read extract 204 of the Social Action compilation at the linked source. What does it suggest that confirmation is sought for an ordinary examination?

questions: How can grace be both a pure gift that does not depend on capacity and something received according to capacity? Compare the passages saying that the blessings themselves become the worthiness and that this is the Day of Grace with those on brackish ground, the polished mirror and the outpouring that comes as soon as capacity is shown.

Why do the readings set faith, guidance and recognition apart from other bounties? Consider the passages that call guidance pure bestowal, the lamp and the sun, and the souls who spent years in worship yet remained deprived. What does this suggest about how a person should regard their own faith and the faith of others?

If the outpouring never ceases, how do the readings account for its seeming absence? Compare the passages on delay, on deprivation through heedlessness, discord, weariness and a depressed mind, and on conduct that blocks the outpourings for others.

What does the image of a magnet add to the language of grace? List the magnets the readings name, such as teaching, pure intention, love, unity and firmness, and ask whether each is a condition, a cause or a sign of confirmation.

How do the readings hold together reliance on confirmation and responsibility for effort? Consider the wind and the rudder, the foreordained bestowal that needs effort, the call for a person of action, and the counsel not to look at one’s own capacity.

What do the images of transformation, the drop and the ocean, the ant and Solomon, the gnat and the eagle, ask of a reader who feels weak? How do the passages linking confirmation with trial and opposition change the meaning of difficulty?
